verses.text: Now there was a certain man in Caesarea, Cornelius by name, a centurion of what was called the Italian Regiment,
a devout man, and one who feared God with all his house, who gave gifts for the needy generously to the people, and always prayed to God.
At about the ninth hour of the day,  he clearly saw in a vision an angel of God coming to him, and saying to him, “Cornelius!”
He, fastening his eyes on him, and being frightened, said, “What is it, Lord?” He said to him, “Your prayers and your gifts to the needy have gone up for a memorial before God.
Now send men to Joppa, and get Simon, who is also called Peter.
He lodges with a tanner named Simon, whose house is by the seaside.
When the angel who spoke to him had departed, Cornelius called two of his household servants and a devout soldier of those who waited on him continually.
Having explained everything to them, he sent them to Joppa.
Now on the next day as they were on their journey, and got close to the city, Peter went up on the housetop to pray at about noon.
He became hungry and desired to eat, but while they were preparing, he fell into a trance.
He saw heaven opened and a certain container descending to him, like a great sheet let down by four corners on the earth,
in which were all kinds of four-footed animals of the earth, wild animals, reptiles, and birds of the sky.
A voice came to him, “Rise, Peter, kill and eat!”
But Peter said, “Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean.”
A voice came to him again the second time, “What God has cleansed, you must not call unclean.”
This was done three times, and immediately the vessel was received up into heaven.
Now while Peter was very perplexed in himself what the vision which he had seen might mean, behold, the men who were sent by Cornelius, having made inquiry for Simon’s house, stood before the gate,
and called and asked whether Simon, who was also called Peter, was lodging there.
While Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said to him, “Behold, three  men seek you.
But arise, get down, and go with them, doubting nothing; for I have sent them.”
Peter went down to the men, and said, “Behold, I am he whom you seek. Why have you come?”

They said, “Cornelius, a centurion, a righteous man and one who fears God, and well spoken of by all the nation of the Jews, was directed by a holy angel to invite you to his house, and to listen to what you say.”
So he called them in and provided a place to stay. On the next day Peter arose and went out with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him.
On the next day they entered into Caesarea. Cornelius was waiting for them, having called together his relatives and his near friends.
When Peter entered, Cornelius met him, fell down at his feet, and worshiped him.
But Peter raised him up, saying, “Stand up! I myself am also a man.”
As he talked with him, he went in and found many gathered together.

He said to them, “You yourselves know how it is an unlawful thing for a man who is a Jew to join himself or come to one of another nation, but God has shown me that I shouldn’t call any man unholy or unclean.
Therefore also I came without complaint when I was sent for. I ask therefore, why did you send for me?”
Cornelius said, “Four days ago, I was fasting until this hour, and at the ninth hour,  I prayed in my house, and behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing,
and said, ‘Cornelius, your prayer is heard, and your gifts to the needy are remembered in the sight of God.
Send therefore to Joppa, and summon Simon, who is also called Peter. He lodges in the house of a tanner named Simon, by the seaside. When he comes, he will speak to you.’
Therefore I sent to you at once, and it was good of you to come. Now therefore we are all here present in the sight of God to hear all things that have been commanded you by God.”
Peter opened his mouth and said, “Truly I perceive that God doesn’t show favoritism;
but in every nation he who fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him.
The word which he sent to the children of Israel, preaching good news of peace by Jesus Christ — he is Lord of all —
you yourselves know what happened, which was proclaimed throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee, after the baptism which John preached;
even Jesus of Nazareth, how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power, who went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him.
We are witnesses of everything he did both in the country of the Jews, and in Jerusalem; whom they also  killed, hanging him on a tree.
God raised him up the third day, and gave him to be revealed,
not to all the people, but to witnesses who were chosen before by God, to us, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead.
He commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that this is he who is appointed by God as the Judge of the living and the dead.
All the prophets testify about him, that through his name everyone who believes in him will receive remission of sins.”
While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell on all those who heard the word.
They of the circumcision who believed were amazed, as many as came with Peter, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was also poured out on the Gentiles.
For they heard them speaking in other languages and magnifying God. Then Peter answered,
“Can anyone forbid these people from being baptized with water? They have received the Holy Spirit just like us.”
He commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to stay some days.

footnotes.content: Caesarea was the Roman administrative heart of Judea—a place where Jewish faith and pagan power collided. That God's Spirit reaches a centurion here, in this very seat of earthly authority, tells us the gospel stops for no border.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Notice what marks Cornelius: not baptism or Torah observance, but a life already turned toward God. He prayed, he gave, and his whole household followed him. The Spirit was already working long before Peter arrived.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three in the afternoon—the hour of prayer. God meets him not in silence or secret, but when Cornelius's heart is already bent toward Heaven. The Lord speaks clearest to those who've already started listening.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here is tenderness: God names Cornelius's prayers and alms as a memorial before Him. Every act of mercy, every whispered prayer from a seeking heart—it rises and is remembered. We are never unseen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The angel gives Cornelius not the full story, but the next step: find Peter. Sometimes the Lord calls us to move forward with only the next stone in view, trusting He will make the path clear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A tanner's house by the sea—the very work of tanning made a Jew ritually unclean by strict law. That Peter lodges there shows he's already leaving behind the old walls. The Spirit prepares his heart before the vision comes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Cornelius doesn't keep this vision to himself or hesitate. He acts at once, trusting what he's heard, and brings those nearest to him—servants and a soldier—into the mystery. Obedience spreads.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Cornelius tells them everything—not to test them, but to invite them into the same trust. When we've met God, we can't help but make room for others to meet Him too.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: While Cornelius obeys below in Caesarea, Peter climbs to pray in Joppa miles away. Both are on their knees. The Lord coordinates His children's steps in ways they cannot yet see—faith is walking the path He's already prepared.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter grows hungry and enters a trance—body and spirit both open, ready. Sometimes we need hunger, or sleep, or stillness to quiet the voice of old certainty and hear what the Spirit truly says.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Heaven opens—not gradually, but suddenly. The sheet descends held by four corners: complete, held safe, lowered to earth. Every wall Peter believed separated clean from unclean is now undone before his eyes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All kinds—beasts and reptiles and birds. Everything once forbidden now present together. The vision is not about food; it's about Peter's heart. Can he eat with those he's called unclean? The Lord is asking him to go further than his law allows.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Kill and eat"—stark and direct. It's not a suggestion or a riddle, but a command from the voice Peter trusts above all others. Yet he refuses. Even Peter must face his own convictions and let them be broken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter's refusal is not rebellious—it's devout. His whole life has been built on holiness understood as separation. To eat what the law forbids feels like betraying the very God he loves. Yet the Lord is calling him to a larger holiness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three times the call returns: "What God has cleansed, you must not call unclean." Not that the law was false, but that God has now done something new. Peter's faithfulness now means accepting what God Himself is redefining.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The three repetitions mirror God's patience and the depth of what needs changing in Peter's mind. Then the sheet is drawn back to heaven—the vision ends, but the lesson remains. Peter is left bewildered and forever changed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter's perplexity is real—he doesn't know what the vision means. Meanwhile, the men Cornelius sent draw near. The Holy Spirit will interpret the vision not through words alone, but through what He's about to do.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The servants call out from the gate, asking their careful question. They don't assume or rush. Even in the midst of obedience, there's room for simple courtesy and respect.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: While Peter ponders, the Spirit speaks with directness: "Three men seek you." Not a debate or a gradual dawning, but the Spirit's clear word cutting through Peter's confusion. The Lord meets us in our perplexity with immediate guidance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Doubting nothing"—go with these men without hesitation. The Spirit's command comes with a reason: "I have sent them." Peter is being asked to trust the Spirit more than his own questions. Sometimes obedience requires we move forward without understanding.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter steps out and identifies himself simply: "I am he whom you seek." No pride, no interrogation. He greets them as those sent by God. Watch how quickly the Spirit's word turns uncertainty into simple, faithful action.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They describe Cornelius: righteous, God-fearing, well-spoken of by all Jews. Here is the paradox Peter must now receive—a Gentile living the very life of faith that the law aims at. If such a man is righteous, what wall remains between him and salvation?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter calls them in, provides lodging, treats them as guests—already breaking custom. And he takes companions from Joppa, witnesses to what God is about to do. Community will anchor what comes next.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Cornelius is not idle or alone when they arrive—he's gathered his whole household, his kindred and friends. He's made room for everyone to hear. Cornelius's faith is not private; it reaches outward to those he loves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Cornelius falls and worships Peter. Such reverence—misplaced, but sincere. In it we see how hungry Cornelius has been for truth, how ready to bow before anyone who might bring him closer to God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter raises him at once: "Stand up! I myself am also a man." Peter's humility mirrors his new understanding—no one stands above another. All are equal before the God who has just shattered the old hierarchy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Many have gathered together—the whole household, eager and quiet, waiting to hear. Peter walks into a room full of hunger for God. This is where the gospel will now go: to the Gentiles, to the peoples the law had marked as outside.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter speaks plainly about what he's learned: it was unlawful for him to come here, but God has shown him not to call any person unholy or unclean. He testifies to his own transformation before he preaches the gospel. Witness always starts with changed hearts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Without complaint"—Peter arrived without the old resistance, without hidden resentment. And now he asks them to explain. He comes as a learner as well as a teacher. Humility opens the way for the Spirit to work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Cornelius recounts his vision with exact detail—four days, the ninth hour again, a man in bright clothing. He's been carrying this moment, turning it over in his heart, ready to tell Peter everything. His readiness to speak mirrors Peter's readiness to listen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The angel's words circle back to what the Lord sees: prayers heard, gifts remembered. Cornelius hasn't been forgotten or overlooked. Every act of worship and mercy rises before God whether or not the worshiper yet knows His full name.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The angel gives the address—Simon the tanner's house by the sea. A specific place in the material world, where one man lodges in another's home. The gospel arrives at particular addresses, in particular rooms, spoken by particular mouths to particular ears.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Now therefore we are all here present in the sight of God"—Cornelius gathers them as a worshiping community, gathered not in a temple but in a home, not yet baptized but already assembled to hear the word. The Spirit was already making them a church.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter begins with the gospel's foundation: God doesn't show favoritism. The highest truth is the simplest—God is not bound by what humans call clean or unclean, near or far. Grace is radically equal.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In every nation, those who fear Him and work righteousness are acceptable. Peter is not saying the law doesn't matter—he's saying God sees the heart first. Righteousness lived out in any language, any land, finds welcome before the throne.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Jesus Christ—he is Lord of all." The gospel Peter announces is not for Israel alone but for all peoples. One Lord, one peace, one gospel crossing all the borders humans draw.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter appeals to what Cornelius would know—the story of Jesus spread through Judea and Galilee. Peter anchors the good news in real events witnessed, proclaimed, remembered. The gospel is not myth but history.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jesus went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil. The portrait here is tender—not Jesus as judge first, but Jesus as healer, liberator, the One whose hand reached every suffering place. God was with Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter and the apostles were witnesses. They saw the work, saw the death by crucifixion—"hanging him on a tree." Witness requires seeing the worst as well as the best, death as well as life. The gospel is proclaimed by those who saw.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God raised him the third day—not after long ages, but the third day. The resurrection is God's immediate answer to death. Jesus didn't stay in the grave; the Father raised Him. Death held no power.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Not to all people, but to witnesses chosen before by God—those who ate and drank with Him after His rising. Witness to resurrection is intimate: they saw Him, broke bread with Him, knew Him alive. That is the foundation of the apostolic word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jesus is appointed Judge of the living and the dead. This comes after grace and healing—the Lord who judges is the Lord who healed, who rose, who shares meals with His own. Justice and mercy are one in Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All the prophets testify about Him—the whole Scripture leans toward Jesus. And through His name everyone who believes receives remission of sins. The gospel's offer is total and universal: forgiveness for all who turn and trust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: While Peter is still speaking—the words are not finished, the prayer not complete—the Holy Spirit falls on all who hear. The Spirit doesn't wait for Peter's eloquence or for the full ritual of the old law. Grace interrupts and moves ahead.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Those of the circumcision who believed are amazed—the Jewish believers witness the Spirit poured on Gentiles just as He fell on them at Pentecost. The moment is unmistakable: God has accepted them. The same gift, no waiting, no gap between Jew and Greek.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They hear them speaking in other languages and magnifying God. The Spirit gives voice and language to the Gentiles, just as He did at Pentecost. The very sign of Pentecost—many tongues, one Spirit—is now repeated for all the peoples.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Can anyone forbid these people from being baptized?" Peter asks the question aloud. He's not asking permission from the law or from human walls—he's asking who would dare stand against what God has done. The answer is: no one. The old barriers are broken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter commanded them baptized in Jesus's name, and they asked him to stay. Readers today hear an echo of this: the gospel still reaches outsiders, still breaks walls of separation, still invites all who believe to join the family. The Spirit's welcome is as radical now as then.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
